parts: Lesson 23: Writing Memos and Letters — Summary

A memo (memorandum) is a brief written message for internal communication within an organisation — from one department or person to another — to share information, updates or instructions. It is written on plain paper or a memo form, not on a letterhead.

Structure: heading (MEMO/MEMORANDUM, date, To, From, Subject); opening — the purpose; body — details, background and action required, often in points; closing — summary of action needed and signature (Sd/-).
How to write: state the subject clearly; come to the point at once; short, simple, direct sentences (personal pronouns are fine); break the message into points; be brief — the reader is busy.

A letter is a formal or informal written message, often to people outside the organisation. Structure: sender's address, date, recipient's address, subject (in formal letters), salutation, body (introduction, main content, conclusion), complimentary close (Yours sincerely/faithfully), signature and name, enclosures.

Letter of complaint: state the complaint clearly and politely without blaming; give references (order/invoice numbers, dates) and details of the defect; attach or mention evidence; say exactly what you want done (replacement, refund, repair).
Letter of enquiry: ask for specific information; quote references of earlier letters or agreements; make the urgency clear.
Letters go on a letterhead and are written in an indirect, formal style, often outside the organisation; memos go on plain paper or a memo form, are direct and are for internal use.
